title: Yudhishthira's Anguish (The Curse of Kunti)
body:
Yudhishthira's Anguish (The Curse of Kunti)

The performative victory of the war brought no peace to Yudhishthira's heart. Instead, the heavy weight of slaughter pressed upon his conscience like a leaden shroud. But the deepest, most devastating blow to his moral equilibrium was yet to fall on the banks of the Yamuna, where the funeral rites were being performed.
Before the assembled family, Kuntidevi stood before her sons. With tears streaming down her aged face, she made the agonizing disclosure that Karna—the bitterest enemy of the Pandavas, the warrior whom they had systematically mocked, hunted, and finally slain under controversial circumstances—was her first-born son, born of Surya prior to her marriage to Pandu. She wept as she admitted her youthful folly of setting him afloat in a sealed box upon the river Yamuna, denying him his legitimate birthright.
This disclosure shattered Yudhishthira. The realization that he had engineered the murder of his own eldest brother—the one to whom he owed absolute allegiance, the one who would have sat upon the throne of Hastinapur while Yudhishthira served his feet—threw him into a vortex of existential despair. Turning his tear-stained face to Kunti, Yudhishthira wept: 'By harboring this secret, you have made me the murderer of my own blood. We fought for a kingdom, yet we have slaughtered the very foundation of our lineage.' In his deep anguish, Yudhishthira pronounced a solemn, historic curse upon all women: 'Henceforth, let it be that no woman in this world shall ever be able to keep a secret.'
The celestial sage Narada, witnessing Yudhishthira's descent into self-pity and grief, approached him to provide metaphysical perspective. He explained how Karna's tragic end was not the result of Yudhishthira's arrows alone, but the inevitable culmination of a complex web of past karma and cosmic curses. Narada detailed the structural collapse of Karna's life:

The Deception of Parasurama: Seeking mastery over the highest weapon, the Brahmastra, Karna had deceived Sage Parasurama by claiming to be a Brahmana. When a stinging worm bored into Karna's thigh and he bore the pain silently to avoid waking his master, Parasurama realised his disciple was a Kshatriya. He cursed Karna that the mantras of the mighty astras would escape his memory in his hour of greatest need.
The Curse of the Brahmana: For accidentally shooting a Brahmana's cow during practice, Karna was cursed that his chariot wheel would sink helplessly into the earth during his final combat, making him vulnerable to his foe.
The Deception of Indra: Lord Indra, seeking to protect his son Arjuna, disguised himself as a Brahmana to beg Karna for his natural armour (Kavacha) and earrings (Kundala), which rendered him impenetrable, systematically reducing his strength.
The Demoralisation by Shalya: King Shalya, serving as Karna's charioteer, kept up a constant psychological assault by consistently underrating Karna's valour and magnifying Arjuna's prowess, depressing Karna's fighting spirit from within.

Narada concluded: 'Karna's pledge to his mother Kunti that he would not kill more than one of the five of you, Parasurama's curse, the anger of the Brahmana whose cow was killed by Karna, the way in which his charioteer Shalya depressed him by underrating his valour, and Sree Krishna's divine stratagems—these combined to bring about Karna's end. Do not grieve believing that you alone caused his death.' Yet, the metaphysical consolidation brought little comfort to Yudhishthira's weeping heart.
